title: Definite objects
seoTitle: Turkmen accusative (-y, -ny) and k, p, ç voicing
intro: This unit is about the object of a verb, the thing you see, buy or eat. Turkmen marks an object with an ending when you mean a particular one, the accusative `-(n)Y`. The ending brings a sound change you met in *mekdebe*: *kitap* → *kitaby*. Then come the pronouns as objects (*meni*, *seni*, *ony*) and where the object goes in the sentence.

sections.title: Some tea or the tea: the accusative -(n)Y

blocks.text: In *Men çaý içýärin* (I drink tea), the object *çaý* has no ending: it means tea in general, some tea, any tea. When you mean a particular one, the one in front of you or one already mentioned, the object takes an ending: *Men çaýy içýärin*, I'm drinking the tea. Grammars call it the accusative. English often shows the same difference with **a** or **some** against **the**.

blocks.label: The accusative: the word ends in … · its last vowel is …
lines: -y   a consonant · a, o, u, y
-i   a consonant · e, ä, i, ö, ü
-ny  a vowel · a, o, u, y
-ni  a vowel · e, ä, i, ö, ü

blocks.text: The vowel is *y* or *i*, never *u* or *ü*, because it ends the word: *öýi*, *dosty* (the rounding rule of [A1 unit 3](a1-u03) leaves a final vowel alone).

items.en: I'm buying apples. (some apples, any apples)

blocks.text: **When the ending is a must.** Names of people and places always take it as objects: *Merdany tanaýaryn*, I know Merdan. So does a noun with *bu*, *şu* or *ol* in front, which is always a particular one: *bu kitaby*, this book. And so do pronouns, in the third section.

blocks.title: Only the object
blocks.text: The ending marks the object, not the subject. In *Kitap stolda* (the book is on the table), the book is the subject and has no ending, even though it is a particular book.

blocks.title: -y or -ny
blocks.text: *ý* is a consonant, so *çaý* takes *-y*: *çaýy*, not *çaýny*. After a vowel the *n* is needed: *almany*, *sürüjini*, *Aýnany*. A final *e* also turns into *ä* before *-ni*, as before the dative: *eje* → *ejäni*.

sections.title: kitap → kitaby: k, p, ç, t before a vowel

blocks.text: When an ending that starts with a vowel follows, a word of two or more syllables that ends in *k*, *p* or *ç* softens it: *k* becomes *g*, *p* becomes *b*, *ç* becomes *j*. The spelling follows the sound. Grammars call this voicing. Before an ending that starts with a consonant, such as *-da*, *-dan* or *-lar*, nothing changes.

blocks.label: Voicing before a vowel
lines: t  →  d     a few words: Aşgabady

blocks.caption: Voicing before a vowel, none before a consonant

blocks.text: **t is different.** Most words in *t* keep it: *surat* → *suraty*, *bilet* → *bileti*. Only a few soften it, and *Aşgabat* is the one you need now: *Aşgabady*, *Aşgabada*.

**One syllable: usually no change.** Short words of one syllable keep their consonant: *at* (horse) → *aty*, *saç* (hair) → *saçy*, *top* (ball) → *topy*. A few one-syllable words have a long vowel, which the spelling doesn't show ([A1 unit 1](a1-u01)), and these do soften: *at* (name) → *ady*, *ýurt* (country) → *ýurdy*. That is why the same word *at* gives two forms.

blocks.title: kitaby, never kitapy
blocks.text: Write what you hear: *kitaby*, not *kitapy*; *çöregi*, not *çöreki*; *agajy*, not *agaçy*. The same change gave *mekdebe* in [A1 unit 7](a1-u07), and it will come back with **my**, **your** and the other possessive endings in [A1 unit 9](a1-u09).

sections.title: Me, you, him: meni, seni, ony

blocks.text: Pronouns as objects always take the accusative. *ol* takes its extra *n* again, as in *onda* and *ondan*: *ony*. *bu* and *şu* standing alone, **this one**, become *muny* and *şuny*. Before a noun they don't change: *bu kitaby*, this book.

items.en: The teacher is listening to us.

blocks.title: Object or dative?
blocks.text: Each verb decides its case. *görmek* (to see), *tanamak* (to know someone), *gowy görmek* (to like), *diňlemek* (to listen to) and *çagyrmak* (to invite) take the accusative: *meni görýär*. *seretmek*, *garaşmak* and *kömek etmek* take the dative: *maňa seredýär*, he's looking at me.

The verb comes last, and an object without an ending sits right before it, almost as one unit with the verb. Time and place words come before that pair: *Men her gün çörek alýaryn*, I buy bread every day. Splitting the pair, as in *Men çörek her gün alýaryn*, sounds wrong.

An object with the accusative ending is freer. It usually comes early, often before the time words, and it can even come before the subject when it is the topic you are talking about: *Çöregi men alýaryn*, I'm the one buying the bread. The word just before the verb is the one in focus.

items.en: I'm the one buying the bread.

blocks.text: **At the market.** Buying **at** a place is buying **from** it, so the shop or the market takes the ablative: *Bazardan alma alýaryn*, I buy apples at the market. To ask a price, say *Bu näçe manat?* (how many manat is this?) or *Bahasy näçe?* (how much is it?). Learn *bahasy* (its price) as a fixed phrase for now; its ending comes in [A1 unit 9](a1-u09).

lines.en: Hello! How much is this melon?
The grapes are cheap. Three manat.
All right. I'll take the melon and the grapes.

blocks.title: A present that means will
blocks.text: *alýaryn* can mean **I'll take** when you decide on the spot, like the plans of [A1 unit 6](a1-u06): *Muny alýaryn*, I'll take this one.

summary: A bare object means some or any: *Çaý içýärin*. A particular one takes `-(n)Y`: *Çaýy içýärin*, *almany*, *sürüjini*.
Names, pronouns and nouns after *bu*, *şu*, *ol* always take the ending as objects: *Aýnany*, *meni*, *bu kitaby*.
Before a vowel, *k*, *p*, *ç* at the end of a longer word become *g*, *b*, *j*: *çöregi*, *kitaby*, *agajy*. Before a consonant they stay: *kitapda*.
*t* stays except in a few words such as *Aşgabat* (*Aşgabady*). One-syllable words keep their consonant (*aty*, horse), except long-vowel ones (*ady*, name).
Pronouns: *meni, seni, ony, bizi, sizi, olary*; *muny*, *şuny* for **this one**.
A bare object goes right before the verb; an object with the ending can move. Buy **at** a place with *-dan*: *bazardan*.
